title: Who is most likely to live in homes that are harder to keep warm?
meta_description: This article explores which groups of people are more likely to live in homes with lower energy efficiency across England and Wales and how that might affect them, using data from Census 2021 and energy performance certificates (EPCs).

breadcrumb.text: Who is most likely to live in homes that are harder to keep warm?

lede: This article explores which groups of people are more likely to live in homes with lower energy efficiency across England and Wales and how that might affect them, using data from Census 2021 and energy performance certificates (EPCs).

body.text: 14 December 2023

With [the energy price cap due to rise in January 2024](https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/energy-price-cap), we have explored who might find it more difficult to heat their homes. To do this, we have used data from energy performance certificates (EPCs) and household information from Census 2021.

Of homes with an EPC, around 8 million homes in England (58%) and 460,000 in Wales (62%) were rated below band C. We have used this as a threshold for a low energy efficiency home, in line with [UK government targets for fuel-poor homes to meet this standard by 2030](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/net-zero-strategy).

We found that households with older adults and those with multiple generations living in them were disproportionately likely to be living in these lower energy efficiency homes. A home with lower energy efficiency may be harder to keep warm and more expensive to heat.
Keeping homes warm enough is particularly important for certain groups, including older people.

However, living in a low energy efficiency home is not automatically a sign of financial vulnerability over winter, with owner-occupied homes and detached homes both more likely to have lower energy efficiency.

People aged 65 years and over were less likely than other age groups to report finding it difficult to afford energy bill payments, according to data from our [Opinions and Lifestyle Survey collected between July and October 2023](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/expenditure/articles/impactofincreasedcostoflivingonadultsacrossgreatbritain/julytooctober2023). However, they were more likely than some younger age groups to report cutting back on gas and electricity usage because of the rising cost of living.

Around 40% of all properties across England and Wales did not have an EPC by 2021, meaning they haven’t been included in this article. As EPCs are only required when a house is let or sold, certain types of homes are more likely to fall into this category.
Other breakdowns of homes' energy efficiency by household characteristics such as employment type, ethnicity, religion, and vehicle ownership are included in our associated data tables.

body.box_text:
What is an energy performance certificate?

A domestic energy performance certificate (EPC) provides a snapshot of your property’s overall energy efficiency and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. It can give an indication of how much your heating, lighting, and use of various common appliances might cost.

EPCs are based on data and assumptions about properties collected by approved domestic energy assessors, who then use government-approved modelling software to produce a score typically ranging from 0 to 100. This normally ranks a property from A to G, with A being the most energy efficient. Homes with lower energy efficiency scores may be harder to keep warm and more expensive to heat, particularly during the winter months.

Homes are only legally required to have an EPC if they are being sold or rented out, so many properties (over 11 million) across England and Wales do not have one, and a home’s energy efficiency may have changed since its latest EPC. Households with no EPC are an unknown quantity and do not necessarily have lower energy efficiency.

An EPC is valid for 10 years. Our data include the latest EPC a property has, even if it is more than 10 years old.

body.h2: Homes with people aged 65 years and above more likely to have lower energy efficiency

body.h2: Homes with people aged 65 years and above more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Census 2021 data contain information on the ages of people living in homes, as well as household composition. These data, when matched with energy performance certificate (EPC) data, showed homes with older age groups tended to have lower energy efficiency.

body.h2: Homes with people aged 65 years and above more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Of homes with EPCs, those where at least one, but not all residents were aged 65 and over were more likely to have lower energy efficiency than homes where all residents were aged 65 years or over.

body.h2: Homes with people aged 65 years and above more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Around 7 in 10 homes where at least one, but not all, people were aged 65 and over across England and Wales had lower energy efficiency (67.7% in England and 69.6% in Wales).

body.h2: Homes with people aged 65 years and above more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: By contrast, this reduced to about 6 in 10 homes where all residents were aged 65 years or over (59.4% in England and 62.8% in Wales).

body.h2: Homes with people aged 65 years and above more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Homes where all occupants were aged under 65 years were the least likely to have lower energy efficiency (57.3% in England, and 60.8% in Wales).

body.h2: Multi-generational homes more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Multi-generational homes more likely to have lower energy efficiency

body.h2: Multi-generational homes more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: We can look more closely at each of these groups, by looking at the ages of the rest of the household occupants. Overall, multi-generational households (those with members across at least three different generations) were most likely to live in homes rated below band C.

body.h2: Multi-generational homes more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Around 7 in 10 multi-generational households (69.3% in England and 70.2% in Wales), with a mixture of children (aged 0 to 15 years), people of working age (aged 16 to 64 years), and people aged 65 and above lived in homes with lower energy efficiency.

body.h2: Multi-generational homes more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Among households with some people aged 65 years and over, those whose other members were all aged 15 years or younger were the least likely to live in homes with lower energy efficiency (63.1% of these households in England, and 61.4% in Wales).

body.h2: Multi-generational homes more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: In England, homes where people were all working age were the least likely to have lower energy efficiency (56.2% of homes). In Wales, homes with people of working age and children were the least likely to have poor energy efficiency (60.5%).

body.h2: Homes with people who were all aged 66 years and above more likely have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Over 700,000 homes in England and more than 45,000 homes in Wales with energy performance certificates (EPCs) were single-family households where everyone was aged 66 years and over.

body.h2: Homes with people who were all aged 66 years and above more likely have lower energy efficiency
body.text: These households were more likely to have lower energy efficiency on census day compared with other household types, with two thirds of these households in England (65.9%) and almost 7 in 10 in Wales (69.2%) living in homes rated below band C.

body.h2: Homes with people who were all aged 66 years and above more likely have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Although households known to have exclusively older occupants account for a minority of the population in England and Wales (close to one in five households in both countries), they are disproportionately likely to have lower energy efficiency compared with other household types.

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Homes with lower energy efficiency may be harder to keep warm making them more expensive to heat, which has a direct impact on households struggling with the cost of living. As the winter weather starts to bite, rising living costs leave many people with difficult choices to make.

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Around two-thirds (69%) of adults in Great Britain who said their cost of living had increased in the last month reported their gas and electricity bills had increased, according to data from the latest [Opinions and Lifestyle Survey](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/datasets/publicopinionsandsocialtrendsgreatbritainhouseholdfinances) (15 to 26 November 2023).

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Further analysis of [Opinions and Lifestyle Survey data](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/expenditure/datasets/impactofincreasedcostoflivingonadultsacrossgreatbritain) from 12 July to 1 October 2023 allowed us to look in more detail at which groups have been most affected by the rising cost of living across Great Britain. We found that groups including lone parents (75%), renters (60%), disabled adults (54%), and Black, African, Caribbean or Black British adults (58%) were more likely to report it was difficult (very difficult or somewhat difficult) to afford their energy payments.

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Notably, though people aged 65 years and above were less likely than those in other age groups to report finding it difficult to afford their energy payments, around 6 in 10 people (59%) aged 65 years and above did report cutting back on household fuel like gas or electricity. This appeared higher than in younger age groups with around a quarter (27%) of those aged 16 to 29 years, around 4 in 10 (42%) of those aged 30 to 49 years and 56% of those aged 50 to 64 years reporting this.

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Analysis of [Census 2021 health data](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/articles/generalhealthbyagesexanddeprivationenglandandwales/census2021#general-health-by-age-and-sex) and [Census 2021 disability data](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/disability/articles/disabilitybyagesexanddeprivationenglandandwales/census2021) has already shown the proportion of people across England and Wales who said they had bad or very bad health, or were considered disabled, increases with age. This means that some people in these older age groups who live in less energy efficient homes and are using less fuel to cope with the cost of living, may be at greater risk of [various adverse outcomes associated with colder homes](https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/weather/warnings-and-advice/seasonal-advice/your-home/keeping-your-home-warm-in-winter).

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Homes should ideally remain at a constant temperature of at least 18 degrees Celsius to reduce the risk of adverse outcomes like various health problems associated with the cold, according to [advice published by the Met Office](https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/weather/warnings-and-advice/seasonal-advice/your-home/keeping-your-home-warm-in-winter). Some of these outcomes can include “a wide range of health conditions, especially respiratory and cardiovascular, as well as poor mental health and unintentional injury”, according to [a report by the Institute for Health Equity](https://www.instituteofhealthequity.org/resources-reports/fuel-poverty-cold-homes-and-health-inequalities-in-the-uk/read-the-report.pdf).

body.h2: Older people most likely to report cutting energy usage amid cost-of-living pressures
body.text: Reducing energy use to cope with increasing living costs in homes with poorer energy efficiency may be particularly dangerous for vulnerable groups like young children, people aged 65 years and over, and people with reduced mobility or underlying health conditions.

body.h2: People living in flats and socially rented accommodation less likely to have hard-to-heat homes
body.text: People living in flats and socially rented accommodation less likely to have hard-to-heat homes

body.h2: People living in flats and socially rented accommodation less likely to have hard-to-heat homes
body.text: Not all people in these vulnerable groups live in homes with lower energy performance certificate (EPC) ratings. We know factors such as age, tenure, construction, and size are important in the energy efficiency of a home, and previous research has also found that the [age of a property is the biggest factor in its energy efficiency](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/ageofthepropertyisthebiggestsinglefactorinenergyefficiencyofhomes/2021-11-01).

body.h2: People living in flats and socially rented accommodation less likely to have hard-to-heat homes
body.text: For example, some of these people may live in properties like [flats, maisonettes, and apartments which are known to typically have better energy efficiency](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/energyefficiencyofhousinginenglandandwales/latest#subnational-statistics). A substantially smaller proportion of people lived in homes like these which had ratings below band C.

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Our data tables include information on energy performance certificate (EPC) ratings of homes by a range of other household characteristics.

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Homes with a mixture of three or more ethnic groups were most likely to have lower energy efficiency, as were homes with any combination of three or more religions.

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Homes with multiple vehicles were more likely to have lower energy efficiency.

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Larger proportions of homes with a mixture of people who were employed, unemployed, or economically inactive were less energy efficient.

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Homes heated by solid fuel (including coal) were highly likely to have lower energy efficiency, yet homes heated by district or communal heat networks were far more likely to have better energy efficiency.

body.h2: Homes with multiple ethnicities or religions more likely to have lower energy efficiency
body.text: Further breakdowns of energy efficiency ratings by characteristics such as household size, heating type, occupation, and occupancy are included in our associated data tables.

To find out more about energy efficiency read [the GOV.UK guidance on saving energy in your home](http://www.gov.uk/energy-grants-calculator). You can also phone the Energy Saving Advice Service on 0300 123 1234 or Home Energy Scotland on 0808 808 2282.

You can find out more about support from government, including support with energy bills and household costs this winter, on the [Help for Households webpage](https://helpforhouseholds.campaign.gov.uk/help-with-your-bills/).
